objectives.outcome: You can calculate the mean of a set of ungrouped values.

items.text: You can calculate the mean of a set of ungrouped values.

items.q: What do you get when you divide $250$ by $5$? Write it as $250 \div 5$.
In a frequency table, what does the frequency column tell you?
items.a: How many times each value or class occurs.

blocks.question: Mr. Furqan scored 70, 62, 55, 94, 79 and 86 marks in his six subjects. He wants ONE number that fairly sums up how well he did overall. What single number would you give him, and how would you get it?
blocks.look_for: Add all six marks together, then divide by 6 — pupils may say 'average' without yet knowing the word or the formula.

items.meaning: $\Sigma x \div n$ — the sum of all values divided by the number of values
means 'summation' — add up everything that follows

blocks.text: $\bar{X} = \dfrac{\Sigma x}{n}$ — sum of values over number of values.

video.title: What is Arithmetic Mean? || Data Handling || C.B.S.E. Grade 7 Mathematics

blocks.text: Add Mr. Furqan's six marks and divide by 6 — that single number is called the mean, and p.237-238 gives it a formula.

items: The mean is one of three measures of central tendency, alongside median and mode (p.237).
Mean = Sum of values $\div$ Number of values.
In symbols, $\bar{X} = \dfrac{\Sigma x}{n}$, where $\Sigma x = x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n$ and $n$ is the total number of observations (p.238).

blocks.title: I do — p.237, Mr. Furqan's scores
blocks.prompt: Find the mean of Mr. Furqan's six scores: $70, 62, 55, 94, 79, 86$.

blocks.text: A pupil who writes $446 \div 6 = 74$ and stops has rounded down instead of carrying the decimal — say the answer is $74.33$, not $74$.

blocks.title: We do — together on the board, p.238 weights
blocks.prompt: Find the mean weight (kg) of 5 students of Class 8: $50, 48, 49, 51, 52$.
steps: Divide by $n$: you fill this in — $\bar{X} = \dfrac{250}{5}$.

items.q: The weight 70 kg is now added to the 5 students' weights: $50, 48, 49, 51, 52, 70$. Find the new mean weight.
Using the grid above (Q5's first row of 10 students), find the mean mark: $68, 84, 75, 82, 68, 90, 62, 88, 76, 93$.
From Q6's table (marks of 20 students in mathematics, Grade VII), find the mean mark of the first row of 10 students: $109, 118, 99, 126, 132, 89, 123, 90, 85, 92$.

checkpoint.question: Calculate the mean of the values $60, 75, 90, 45, 80$.

exit_ticket.q: State the formula for the mean in symbols.

sections.reteach_rule: If more than a third of the class divides by the wrong count of values, redo the Mr. Furqan worked example on p.237 before the next period.

blocks.text: $\bar{X} = \dfrac{\Sigma x}{n}$ — count the values, add them, then divide.

items.text: State how the mean of a data set is found: (A) adding all values and multiplying by the count (B) adding all values and dividing by the count (C) taking the largest value (D) taking the middle value
Find the mean mark of the second row of 10 students in Q5's table: $73, 79, 88, 73, 60, 93, 71, 59, 85, 75$.

items: Answers are checked at the start of the next period.

draw_order: Write $\bar{X} = \dfrac{\Sigma x}{n}$ at the top of the board.

mistakes.you_ask: Is 446 the total of all six marks, or is it the mean? What do you still need to do to that number?

mistakes.pupil_says: I divided 250 by 6 to get the mean weight of the 5 students.
mistakes.you_ask: How many students' weights did you actually add together? Does your divisor match that count?

mistakes.pupil_says: The mean must be a whole number.
mistakes.you_ask: When we added 70 kg to the five weights and divided by 6, what did we get — was it whole?

differentiation.stuck: Let them tally the sum on the board with you, one value at a time, before dividing.
differentiation.barrier: Long division with larger totals — allow a written column method or a times-table chart.
differentiation.early: Ask them to find the mean of the full row of 10 marks from Q5's table by hand, showing all steps.

homework_key.answer: (B) — adding all values and dividing by the count is the definition of the mean.
